questions.q: Which trading calendar is used as the reference for aligning all 13 raw CSVs?
options: The VIX calendar
SPY's trading calendar
The CBOE options expiration calendar
Each ETF's own independent calendar
questions.explain: Every ticker is reindexed onto SPY's trading calendar, since SPY has the longest clean history, so dates don't silently misalign across the panel.

questions.q: How are missing-day gaps in the raw data handled?
options: Interpolated linearly across any gap, however long
Forward-filled for at most one session, never further, and flagged
Dropped entirely from the dataset
Replaced with the sector average for that day
questions.explain: Gaps are forward-filled for at most one session and flagged, rather than silently interpolated across a real, longer gap.

questions.q: Why are log returns preferred over simple percentage returns for this analysis?
options: They are always smaller in magnitude
They are additive across time and better match the near-lognormal behavior of asset prices, keeping rolling-window statistics well-behaved
They eliminate the need for adjusted close prices
They remove fat tails from the return distribution
questions.explain: Log returns sum across periods (today's log return plus tomorrow's equals the two-day log return) and better match how prices actually behave, making rolling statistics well-behaved.

questions.q: What does the exploratory correlation matrix across the 11 sectors reveal, and why does it matter?
options: Correlations are mostly negative, supporting a long-only strategy
Correlations are almost all positive and often high (0.6-0.9), confirming a shared market factor — which is why the strategy is dollar-neutral and cross-sectional
Correlations are exactly zero, meaning sectors move independently
Correlation cannot be computed because the universe size changes over time
questions.explain: High, mostly-positive pairwise correlations show a dominant shared market factor, which is exactly why SR-5 is built dollar-neutral and cross-sectional rather than simply long sectors.

questions.q: What does 'point-in-time data' mean as applied to this dataset?
options: Data sampled once per calendar quarter
Data that only ever includes names and values that actually existed as of a given date — never hindsight additions like XLRE or XLC before their launch
Data adjusted retroactively using current index membership
Data recorded only at market close, never intraday
questions.explain: Point-in-time data means the feature-and-model code only ever sees the names that existed as of a given date — no backfilling securities before they launched.
